questions.q: What three components does a real, testable performance requirement need?
options: A budget, a deadline, and a stakeholder sign-off
A screenshot, a test script, and a sandbox
A metric, a numeric target, and a load condition
A governor limit, an Apex class, and a trigger
questions.explain: A real performance requirement names a metric (e.g., page load time), a numeric target (e.g., under 3 seconds), and the condition under which that target applies (e.g., for 95% of requests with 200 concurrent users). Missing any of the three makes it untestable.

questions.q: What is the difference between response time and throughput?
options: Response time measures how long a single transaction takes; throughput measures how many transactions a system processes per unit of time
Response time only applies to batch jobs; throughput only applies to page loads
They are two names for the same measurement
Throughput is a security metric, not a performance metric
questions.explain: Response time is about one user's single transaction. Throughput is about overall volume processed per unit of time — a system can have great response time for one user and poor throughput under concurrent load, since they measure different things.

questions.q: Why do asynchronous Apex transactions (queueable, batch, future, Bulk API) get a larger CPU-time budget than synchronous transactions?
options: Async transactions are exempt from all governor limits
Because Salesforce charges extra for synchronous Apex, so sync has a smaller budget to encourage upgrades
Because async transactions never touch the database
Because async work isn't holding a user's browser open waiting for a response, so it's expected to run longer and is budgeted accordingly
questions.explain: Synchronous Apex runs inline while a user waits, so its CPU-time ceiling is smaller to keep the platform responsive for everyone. Asynchronous work (queueable, batch, future, Bulk API) isn't blocking a live user session and is expected to do more work, so it gets a larger CPU-time allowance.

questions.q: Why do Salesforce's governor limits exist on a multi-tenant platform?
options: To generate additional licensing revenue for Salesforce
To protect shared infrastructure, so that no single org's runaway process degrades performance for other customers on the same infrastructure
To prevent customers from writing any custom Apex code at all
They only exist in sandbox orgs, not production
questions.explain: Because many customers share the same underlying infrastructure in Salesforce's multi-tenant architecture, governor limits exist specifically to stop one org's inefficient or runaway process from consuming resources that would otherwise degrade performance for every other tenant.

questions.q: A team is building a data-loading integration that will insert hundreds of thousands of records. Based on this lesson, which approach best fits the volume?
options: Build it against the standard synchronous REST API, one record per call
Use only declarative Flow automation to avoid governor limits entirely
Use Bulk API (or Bulk API 2.0), which runs under a separate, larger CPU-time allowance intended for large-volume operations
Split the load evenly across multiple standard users logged in simultaneously
questions.explain: Bulk API and Bulk API 2.0 exist specifically for large-volume record operations and run against a separate, larger CPU-time allowance than a single synchronous transaction — which is why high-volume data loading should be built against Bulk API rather than the standard synchronous API.
